findings.title: Findings converge on the handoff between a DatabaseService.submit() write and the core service's in-memory state
findings.why_it_matters: The core service keeps two committed copies of the same facts: the database rows and its in-memory declarations, entity state and revision counter. Every write path (the running-time commit and every `set()`) goes "await `submit()`, then update memory and bump the revision", and the ledger never says who owns the step between. Three findings hit that one gap from different sides: a write that commits after its caller was cancelled or timed out (Finding 2), two concurrent `set()` calls whose commits and publishes land in opposite orders (Finding 6), and a failed commit or failed init whose pending values and memory view are left undefined (Finding 7). Each proposes its own local rule: a re-read, a lock, an ordering sentence. Together they ask whether the design should have two committed states at all, or one place where a committed write and its published value are made the same thing. Is this a structural question about the handoff that should be settled once, rather than three patches? The re-evaluation may also conclude some of these edges are limitations to accept and document.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the write-to-memory handoff before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions the re-evaluation must answer: which copy is authoritative after a write whose caller never saw its outcome; who publishes a committed value and in what order relative to other writes; what a failed or timed-out running-time commit leaves in memory, in the DB, and in the instance's status; whether the commit should run inside the startup timeout at all; and which of these edges are worth handling versus documenting as limitations.
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate the write-to-memory handoff before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions the re-evaluation must answer: which copy is authoritative after a write whose caller never saw its outcome; who publishes a committed value and in what order relative to other writes; what a failed or timed-out running-time commit leaves in memory, in the DB, and in the instance's status; whether the commit should run inside the startup timeout at all; and which of these edges are worth handling versus documenting as limitations.
findings.choice_reason: re-evaluate is fine; asked whether the DB-as-source-of-truth milestone (spec 132) would simplify it

findings.title: A started write outlives its cancelled caller, so DB and memory diverge (commit inside the startup timeout; set() under restart mode)
findings.why_it_matters: `submit()` deliberately runs a started write to completion "because it may commit", and a cancelled caller's future is simply dropped. So "the write raised" and "the write committed" are not the only outcomes: the caller can see a cancellation or `TimeoutError` while the row is committed. Two paths in this design hit that third outcome. (1) The running-time commit sits inside `anyio.fail_after(startup_timeout)`. If the deadline fires mid-transaction, the instance goes `FAILED` through `shutdown_instance`, while the DB now holds the new declaration set and memory never swapped. Parent D9's promise that a failed init "never touches the persisted set" is broken, and the next listing or restart silently adds or removes HA entities. (2) A `restart`-mode handler that is cancelled while its `set()` awaits the write leaves the DB holding the new value while memory and HA hold the old one; after the next boot HA sees a value it was never sent. The ledger's carried rule "a cancelled run leaves state unchanged" (Assumed, parent D7) is false once the write has started.
findings.recommended: A: Run the running-time commit after the `fail_after` block (bounded by `submit()`'s own timeout and shielded from outer cancellation so its outcome is always known), have the commit and each `set()` write update memory and the revision inside the write coroutine after the commit succeeds, and correct the carried D7 rule to "a cancelled run leaves state unchanged unless its `set()` write had already started, in which case it takes effect".
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The dispatch entry point #4219 calls has no stated contract for "running and declares this key"
findings.why_it_matters: Parent D5 (ratified) requires the command route to accept only a key the instance currently declares while it is `running`, and to return a typed conflict for each case. The route is #4219's, but it calls this issue's in-process dispatch entry point, and the ledger only says "Dispatch: D1". The core service holds committed declarations for every instance, down ones included (parent D9), so "declared" does not imply "running"; running-ness lives in `AppRegistry`. Nothing says which component checks what, what the entry point returns, or that "dispatched" means "published", not "ran" (a `single`-mode busy drop or a listener cancelled mid-reload ends in a near-miss record, not an error). #4219 would have to reverse-engineer this. The backpressure-drop concern the critic raised does not hold as stated: `Listener.backpressure` defaults to `BLOCK` (`src/hassette/bus/listeners.py:117`) and parent D12 exposes only the execution mode on `add_*`, so `DROP_NEWEST` applies only if the build chose to expose it; the contract should still say these listeners are `BLOCK`.
findings.recommended: A: Add to D1 the entry point's contract: it checks the registry status is `running` and the key is in the instance's committed declarations, publishes with no await between check and publish, and returns a typed result (`dispatched`, `not_running`, `not_declared`); "dispatched" means published, not ran, and mode drops are visible only as near-miss records; declaration listeners are registered with `BLOCK` backpressure.
findings.chosen: A: Add to D1 the entry point's contract: it checks the registry status is `running` and the key is in the instance's committed declarations, publishes with no await between check and publish, and returns a typed result (`dispatched`, `not_running`, `not_declared`); "dispatched" means published, not ran, and mode drops are visible only as near-miss records; declaration listeners are registered with `BLOCK` backpressure.

findings.title: "The handler called set() during that run" has no run identity
findings.why_it_matters: The carried parent D7 rule says the framework sets the commanded switch value after the handler returns, unless the handler called `set()` during that run; under `parallel` the last-completed run wins. The only mechanism the ledger names is "a framework wrapper around the handler that keeps its signature for DI" (D1 table). A flag on the handle is wrong under `parallel` and `restart`: run A's `set()` would make run B skip its auto-set. Run-scoped tracking needs a per-invocation identity, and the ledger doesn't say what it is or how `set()` finds it from a sync handler on a worker thread or from a task the handler spawned. If it is lost, the framework overwrites the value the handler chose, which D7 says must never happen. Existing code helps: `SyncExecutor.submit` copies the caller's contextvars into the worker (`src/hassette/core/sync_executor.py:182-198`), so a contextvar holding a mutable per-run cell would be visible in sync handlers.
findings.recommended: A: Reopen parent D7 toward its option B: the handler must set the switch state itself, and the framework never auto-sets, so no run identity is needed.
findings.chosen: A: Reopen parent D7 toward its option B: the handler must set the switch state itself, and the framework never auto-sets, so no run identity is needed.
findings.choice_reason: peers' approach sounds simpler and cleaner; asked why parent D7 went the other way and what the downside is

findings.title: The startup prune deletes switch state on an inference from config, with no guard for an empty or wrong config
findings.why_it_matters: The prune deletes declarations and the switch and sensor state hassette is the single source of truth for (parent D6), for any instance absent from the loaded config. It cannot tell "removed on purpose" from "config came from the wrong place". If a restart loads a config with no apps (a wrong Docker volume, an emptied `[apps]` section), every instance is absent and everything is deleted; switch values reset to their initial value and cannot be recovered. One trigger the data-integrity critic raised does not exist: an invalid manifest does not drop out of the loaded set, it fails the whole config load (`ConfigError` at `src/hassette/config/config.py:588-589`), so hassette never reaches the prune. A renamed or typoed `instance_name` surviving a restart is the case parent D13 already ratified ("safe until the next restart"). What remains unratified is the empty or wrong config.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a restart with an empty or wrong apps config deletes every instance's declarations and switch state, recorded per instance in the log.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a restart with an empty or wrong apps config deletes every instance's declarations and switch state, recorded per instance in the log.

findings.title: Concurrent set() calls can commit and publish in opposite orders
findings.why_it_matters: The single-writer queue orders DB writes, but the publish (memory update and revision bump) happens in each caller after `submit()` returns. Two `set()` calls on one handle can go: commit A, commit B, publish B, publish A. Memory and HA end at A while the DB holds B, so after a restart the persisted value differs from the last value HA saw.
findings.recommended: B: Have the write coroutine update memory and bump the revision itself after commit, so the single writer's queue order is the publish order.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: What a failed commit leaves in memory, and what happens to pending set() values, is unstated
findings.why_it_matters: Pending declarations and pending `set()` values are held on the integration resource and written in the commit. If the service updates memory before the commit completes, a failed init leaves values in memory the DB never took, visible to #4219's listing. If it updates only after, the handle's restored state read during `on_initialize` must come from the committed row, not the pending value. The ledger names neither.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The prune and the in-memory load have no stated order or placement
findings.why_it_matters: The core service holds every instance's committed declarations in memory, loaded from the DB, and the prune runs "once at app bootstrap". If the service loads memory before the prune (a natural place for a `Service` is its own init, which runs before app bootstrap), pruned instances stay in memory and #4219 serves them. Separately, if the prune sits inside `bootstrap_apps`, its empty-manifests early return decides whether an empty config prunes everything or nothing, and the ledger doesn't say which.
findings.chosen: In the Startup prune bullet (design.md:39), state that the prune runs in the core service's startup step before it loads declarations and state into memory, so memory is loaded from the pruned DB; that it does not sit behind `bootstrap_apps`' empty-manifests early return; and that a prune failure fails the service's startup (loud failure, per Posture).

findings.title: The one-transaction replace needs an explicit BEGIN and rollback on an autocommit connection
findings.why_it_matters: D4 and parent D9 depend on "upsert kept rows, delete the rest" happening in one transaction. The write connection is opened with `isolation_level=None`, so each statement autocommits unless the code issues `BEGIN` itself, and `submit()` provides no transaction. Written as separate `execute` calls, an exception between them leaves the set half-replaced, and a cancel can leave an open transaction on the shared connection for the next write to join. Happy-path tests won't catch it.
findings.chosen: In the Persistence bullet (design.md:33-34), state that the replace-set commit (and the state-row delete it includes) runs as `SQL_BEGIN` … commit inside `try/except BaseException: safe_rollback(...); raise`, following `database_retention.py`, with a test that forces a failure after the upsert and before the delete and checks the old set is intact.

findings.title: The new table lands in a database the docs call safe to delete
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a user whose telemetry DB can be recreated at any time and who does not mind, which the existing tables are designed for. Every table in `hassette.db` today is regenerable telemetry, and the troubleshooting page tells users so: "**Safe to delete.** Deleting `hassette.db` only removes telemetry history." With this issue, the same file holds the only copy of switch state and sensor values. A user who follows that advice resets every switch to its initial value and every sensor to `unknown`, and the doc that told them to do it becomes false. Two other paths the critic named do not apply as stated: the version-0 recreate only fires on a file with `user_version` 0, which a migrated DB never has (`database_service.py:476-483`), and `restore_snapshot` only runs when the DB is missing after an add-on backup restore (`database_snapshot.py:78-100`), where returning to the backup's switch state is what a restore means. Retention and the size failsafe walk only the tables in `retention_targets.py`, so the new table is safe unless someone adds it there.
findings.recommended: A: Change the troubleshooting "Safe to delete" paragraph and the new integration-entities page (D9) to say deleting `hassette.db` also resets declared switch and sensor values (declarations come back at the next start), and state in the Persistence bullet that the table is never a retention or failsafe target.
findings.chosen: A: Change the troubleshooting "Safe to delete" paragraph and the new integration-entities page (D9) to say deleting `hassette.db` also resets declared switch and sensor values (declarations come back at the next start), and state in the Persistence bullet that the table is never a retention or failsafe target.
findings.choice_reason: agreed; wants a research spike on keeping runtime state separate from logs/telemetry, which may resolve log-retention tension

findings.title: The harness's in-memory store can't fail, so failure paths are untestable through it
findings.why_it_matters: The harness runs no `DatabaseService` and backs the core service with an in-memory store "that keeps the same commit and `set()` semantics". The risks this design cares about are commit failure, `TimeoutError` from `submit`, and a failed `set()` leaving memory unchanged; an in-memory store never fails, so app authors can't test their handling of a raising `set()` (which the Posture makes loud), and the framework's own commit and cancel paths need tests against the real write queue.
findings.recommended: B: Test the commit, cancel and failed-`set()` paths with framework integration tests against the real `DatabaseService`, and add no public fault seam until an app author asks for one.
findings.chosen: B: Test the commit, cancel and failed-`set()` paths with framework integration tests against the real `DatabaseService`, and add no public fault seam until an app author asks for one.

findings.title: No logs named for commit, prune or dispatch-rejection outcomes
findings.why_it_matters: The service runs unattended failure modes (commit failure, the startup prune, a press rejected or dropped), and the ledger names only near-miss rows for mode drops. "I pressed it and nothing happened" or "my switch reset" can't be diagnosed weeks later without a record of what was committed, pruned or rejected.
findings.chosen: Under Posture → Hardening (design.md:59), name the log points: INFO for each running-time commit (instance, counts added/kept/removed); WARNING for each pruned `(app_key, instance_name)` with row counts; WARNING when the dispatch entry point rejects a press (`not_running`/`not_declared`); ERROR for a failed framework post-handler write (already in Assumed); structured fields via `extra=`.

findings.title: A shut-down instance's handles can still write the new instance's rows
findings.why_it_matters: The state row key `(app_key, instance_name, key, platform)` is shared by every incarnation of an instance. D7 closes the declaration window per object, but nothing closes `set()` on the old object's handles. A task leaked from a shut-down instance (one `shutdown_instance` flags needs-restart because work may still be running) can call `set()`, overwrite the new instance's persisted value and bump the revision, so a sensor or switch flips to the old app's value with no log.
findings.recommended: A: `set()` raises (a `HassetteError` naming the instance) when the handle's owning `self.integration` resource has shut down, checked against that resource's existing lifecycle status.
findings.chosen: A: `set()` raises (a `HassetteError` naming the instance) when the handle's owning `self.integration` resource has shut down, checked against that resource's existing lifecycle status.

findings.title: The command topic is an internal event any app can publish
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: apps that are not mutually trusted, which does not describe a solo personal install. D1-A accepted that "the command event is visible on the bus to any listener"; it also means any app can `send_event` on that topic, which skips the entry point's running and declared checks and runs another app's handler with an arbitrary value. Parent D5 already accepted that anyone with the web API token can press any entity.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: any app can publish the internal command topic and run another app's declared handler, bypassing the running/declared checks.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: any app can publish the internal command topic and run another app's declared handler, bypassing the running/declared checks.

findings.title: Prune and commit have no recorded behavior for the instance reload/stop path
Findings converge on handle ownership (the `_owners` map and `CLOSED_STATUSES`)
findings.why_it_matters: "May this handle still act on its instance's committed state?" is answered in three places by three partial rules. `IntegrationService` records the last committing `Integration` in `_owners` at commit and never releases it. `Integration.set_state` separately checks its own lifecycle status against `CLOSED_STATUSES`. `Integration.read_state` checks neither. All three critics landed on this from different directions: two checks for one question (Finding 5), the never-released `_owners` entry pinning a stopped `App` in memory (Finding 6), reads that skip the ownership check that writes enforce (Finding 7), and a `set()` in `on_shutdown` after a failed commit that fails the owner check with an error that doesn't say why (Finding 8). Each proposes its own local patch: a weakref, a read-side check, a message tweak, a release hook. The question for the user is whether this points to the ownership mechanism itself being shaped wrong, to be re-evaluated as a whole, rather than patched four times. Re-evaluation is open-ended: it includes whether separate ownership tracking is needed at all, and whether some of these failure modes (leaked handles, reads after a reload) are limitations to accept and document.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate handle ownership before addressing Findings 5-8 individually. Open questions: does the service need to track owners at all, or can one side own liveness? When does ownership end (shutdown, replacement, failed commit)? Should reads follow the same rule as writes? Which of the leaked-handle cases are worth handling versus documenting?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate handle ownership before addressing Findings 5-8 individually. Open questions: does the service need to track owners at all, or can one side own liveness? When does ownership end (shutdown, replacement, failed commit)? Should reads follow the same rule as writes? Which of the leaked-handle cases are worth handling versus documenting?

findings.title: Every app instance, including those that declare nothing, now runs a DB write, a revision bump and an INFO log on each start
findings.why_it_matters: `initialize_instance` calls `inst.integration.commit_declarations()` for every instance, and `commit_job` has no empty-set shortcut. An app that never touches `self.integration` still submits a write to the single DB writer, runs BEGIN/upsert-over-nothing/SELECT/DELETE/COMMIT, bumps `revision`, and logs "0 added, 0 kept, 0 removed" at INFO. If that write times out before it starts (`write_submit_timeout_seconds`) or fails, the app goes `FAILED`; if it wedges, the app stays in `STARTING` (D10.5's accepted wedge, now applied to every app). The revision bump also tells #4220 consumers something changed on every app restart when nothing did. The Posture ("ships outright, nothing consumes the feature") reasons about who uses the feature, not about who pays for it.
findings.recommended: A: Before submitting, skip the commit when the instance declared nothing and the service holds no committed set for it: close the window, no write, no revision bump, no INFO log. An instance that had a set and now declares none still commits, so its rows are deleted. Add a test that a non-declaring app causes no `submit()`.
findings.chosen: A: Before submitting, skip the commit when the instance declared nothing and the service holds no committed set for it: close the window, no write, no revision bump, no INFO log. An instance that had a set and now declares none still commits, so its rows are deleted. Add a test that a non-declaring app causes no `submit()`.
findings.choice_reason: Clear-cut; picked by the session and listed to the user before the contested questions

findings.title: The ledger's D10 cancel/stop guarantees and D1's execution modes have no test pinning them
findings.why_it_matters: D10 is the ledger's load-bearing decision ("settle the write/memory relationship once"), and the behaviors most likely to regress silently are untested: the shield and out-of-timeout commit (D10.2), a cancelled caller's started `set()` taking effect (D10.4), a stop during an in-flight commit (D10.5), concurrent `set()` ordering (D10.1), pending values discarded after a failed commit (D10.3). Nothing covers D1's `mode=` through the listener, prune failure failing service startup, or an empty-declaration commit either. If someone later removes `asyncio.shield` or moves the commit back inside the startup timeout, nothing fails. The harness store never fails, so it can't catch any of this.
findings.chosen: Add real-`DatabaseService` tests gated with `asyncio.Event`s, following `.claude/rules/regression-test-patterns.md`: (1) cancel `initialize_instance` while a gated `commit_job` is in flight; the set still lands in memory and SQLite. (2) Cancel a `set()` after its write started; memory and the row both update. (3) A `set()` queued but not started when its caller is cancelled changes nothing. (4) Two concurrent `set()` calls leave memory equal to the last committed row. (5) A stop landing during an in-flight commit keeps the committed set. (6) After a failed commit, a retried commit starts with no stale pending values. (7) A `single`-mode button pressed while its handler runs records a `busy` drop. (8) A prune failure fails `IntegrationService` startup. (9) An empty-declaration commit, asserting whichever behavior Finding 2 settles.

findings.title: Memory holds attribute objects the caller and the handle can mutate, and the no-op check compares Python objects rather than what SQLite stores
findings.why_it_matters: `check_attributes` makes only a shallow `dict(attributes)`, so nested lists and dicts stay shared with the caller. `handle.attributes` (and `handle.state.attributes`) returns the committed dict itself; `EntityState` is a frozen dataclass, but its `attributes` field is a plain mutable dict at runtime. So `sw.attributes["history"].append(x)` or `sw.attributes["x"] = 1` edits committed memory with no write. The next `set()` with those attributes then compares equal in `set_job`, returns without writing, and never bumps the revision: the row and whatever #4219/HA reads stay stale while the handle shows the new value, until the value changes. Separately, the no-op check uses Python equality, so `True == 1 == 1.0` and `set(5, attributes={"armed": True})` after `{"armed": 1}` writes nothing. JSON round-trips also differ from memory (int keys become strings, tuples become lists), so a restored state differs from the live one.
findings.recommended: A: Normalize attributes through a JSON round-trip in `check_attributes` (a fresh deep copy in persisted form), and have the handle return a copy (or read-only view over a copy) so callers can't edit committed memory.
findings.chosen: A: Normalize attributes through a JSON round-trip in `check_attributes` (a fresh deep copy in persisted form), and have the handle return a copy (or read-only view over a copy) so callers can't edit committed memory.
findings.choice_reason: Clear-cut; picked by the session and listed to the user before the contested questions

findings.title: Two separate "closed handle" checks exist because ownership is never released
findings.why_it_matters: `Integration.set_state` checks its lifecycle status against `CLOSED_STATUSES`; `IntegrationService.set_job` checks `_owners.get(instance) is not owner`, with a comment explaining why both are needed. Two rules in two classes answer one question, from two partial views: "I am still the last committer" and "my lifecycle status isn't closed". A stopped owner with no replacement passes the service check and is caught only by the status check. `CLOSED_STATUSES` is one more constant to keep in step with the lifecycle's statuses.
findings.recommended: A: Have `Integration` release its ownership on shutdown (`service.release(self)` pops `_owners` if it is still this owner), make `set_job`'s owner check the single rule, and delete `CLOSED_STATUSES`.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: `_owners` keeps the last committing `Integration`, and through it the whole `App`, alive after a stop or config removal
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: long-running installs that hot-reload apps or edit config often. `self._owners[instance] = owner` is never cleared on stop, and `_entities`/`_owners` for an instance removed from config at runtime are kept until the next restart (pruning runs only in `on_initialize`). A stopped app's object graph (bus, scheduler, api, user attributes) stays reachable. Reloads replace the entry on the next commit of the same instance name, so the retention is bounded by the number of instance names that stop without restarting.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a stopped or de-configured instance's last `App` stays in memory until restart.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A handle's `state` read has no ownership check, unlike `set()`
findings.why_it_matters: With the window closed, `read_state` returns the service's committed state for `(app_key, instance_name)` whatever the owner. A handle leaked past a reload reads the new instance's value; a handle of an instance whose commit failed reads the previous run's value. `is_on` and `value` then silently report another instance's state.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a handle used after its instance stopped or was replaced reads the current committed state of that instance name.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A `set()` inside `on_shutdown` after a failed commit raises an error that doesn't say the commit failed
findings.why_it_matters: The Build call to run shutdown hooks after a failed commit means a hook that calls `handle.set(...)` (a natural "offline" write) hits the owner check, because `_owners` still holds the previous owner, and raises `IntegrationHandleClosedError` naming only the instance and key. It reads as an app bug rather than the framework's commit failure. The normal-stop path works: hooks run before the `Integration` child goes `STOPPING`.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: after a failed commit, a `set()` in `on_shutdown` raises `IntegrationHandleClosedError` without naming the failed commit.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A process exit landing during the commit is followed by a late RUNNING that `dispatch_command` would trust
findings.why_it_matters: `initialize_instance` checks admission before the commit snapshot, awaits the commit, then writes RUNNING unconditionally. `AppRegistry.set_status` accepts RUNNING over STOPPING when the entry still has its `App`. `dispatch_command` decides "running" from exactly that registry status, so in the window before `clear_all` it would publish a press to a bus being torn down and return `DISPATCHED`. `shutdown_all`'s docstring says of these late statuses that "nothing acts on that state", which stops being true once #4219 calls `dispatch_command`. The critic's trigger includes manual stops and reloads; those hold the app-key lock, as do the start paths that reach `initialize_instance`, so only process exit (`shutdown_all`, no lock) can interleave. The orchestrator's pre-commit reasoning holds on that point.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: during process exit, a press arriving between a late RUNNING and `clear_all` can be reported `DISPATCHED` without running. Correct `shutdown_all`'s "nothing acts on that state" to name it.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: during process exit, a press arriving between a late RUNNING and `clear_all` can be reported `DISPATCHED` without running. Correct `shutdown_all`'s "nothing acts on that state" to name it.

findings.title: The harness builds command events itself instead of going through `dispatch_command`
findings.why_it_matters: `simulate_button_press` and `simulate_switch_toggle` re-derive "is it declared" and build `IntegrationCommandEvent` themselves, never calling `dispatch_command`, the D1 entry point #4219 will call. There are two copies of "declared?" and of event construction that can drift, and no test drives dispatch, then bus, then handler end to end: `not_running`/`not_declared` are tested only against a mocked `send_event` and a `MagicMock` registry. User tests written against the harness won't reflect changes #4219 makes to dispatch.
findings.recommended: A: Move the declared check and `IntegrationCommandEvent.create` into one service method (for example `build_command_event`) used by `dispatch_command` and the harness; only the registry-status check stays production-only.
findings.chosen: A: Move the declared check and `IntegrationCommandEvent.create` into one service method (for example `build_command_event`) used by `dispatch_command` and the harness; only the registry-status check stays production-only.
findings.choice_reason: Clear-cut; picked by the session and listed to the user before the contested questions

findings.title: D12's "pending, else restored if it fits, else default" precedence is written twice
findings.why_it_matters: `Integration.read_state` and `IntegrationService.initial_state` each implement the same precedence, and `read_state` carries a comment saying it must match. If D12 or the default rules change, a handle can show a value the commit then resets, which is the exact case D12 exists to prevent. (The critic counted three copies; `restore_state` is decoding, not precedence, so it's two.)
findings.recommended: A: Add a pure `resolve_state(declaration, pending, existing)` in `declarations.py` that returns the state and whether it reset; `read_state` and `initial_state` both call it, and the service logs the D12 WARNING when it reset.
findings.chosen: A: Add a pure `resolve_state(declaration, pending, existing)` in `declarations.py` that returns the state and whether it reset; `read_state` and `initial_state` both call it, and the service logs the D12 WARNING when it reset.
findings.choice_reason: Clear-cut; picked by the session and listed to the user before the contested questions

findings.title: The service's write path has several pass-through layers whose main reason is the harness subclass
findings.why_it_matters: A commit goes `commit_declarations` → `commit_instance` → `run_write` → `commit_job` → `persist_instance_set` → `integration_store.replace_instance_set`; a `set()` is seven hops. `persist_instance_set`, `persist_state` and `prune_and_load` are one-line pass-throughs that exist so `HarnessIntegrationService` can override them, and the class docstring says so. The harness's `run_write` awaits the job inline in the caller's task, so shield and cancellation behave differently there than in production. Whoever adds a fifth write path must remember the subclass.
findings.recommended: B: Leave the layering as is.
findings.chosen: B: Leave the layering as is.

findings.title: The handle classes and the sync facade carry more public surface than the ledger needs
findings.why_it_matters: The ledger says one class per platform; `handles.py` adds two base classes for three leaves, and `IntegrationButton` and `IntegrationSwitch` duplicate the `subscription` field and `__init__`. A switch exposes `state`, `attributes`, `is_on` and `declaration`; `attributes` is `state.attributes` and `is_on` is `bool(state.value)`. The repo's "keep the public surface small" rule applies. `IntegrationSyncFacade` is a full `Resource` for four methods, and its `set(handle, ...)` doesn't use the integration it wraps; the parity test covers only the `add_*` mirrors (a harness test does exercise `set`).
findings.recommended: B: Keep the handles and facade as built.

findings.title: `add_*` validates the key, then the declare coroutine validates it again
findings.why_it_matters: `add_button`/`add_switch`/`add_sensor` call `check_declarable` eagerly so errors raise at the call, then `declare_with_handler`/`declare_sensor` call it again because the window may have closed before the coroutine runs. `declare_sensor` is `async` with no await, only to keep the awaited signature. Two sites to keep in step.

findings.title: Two ledger invariants hold only outside narrow windows
findings.why_it_matters: (i) "A declaration never exists without its listener": `declare_with_handler` inserts the declaration, then awaits `register_listener`. A commit snapshot taken in that gap, only possible from a task that outlives init, captures the declaration, and a failed registration then deletes it locally after it was committed. (ii) D10.3 says a handle reads its latest pending value during init; `commit_declarations` clears `_pending` and closes the window before the write lands, so a read during the commit await (for example from a bus listener registered in `on_initialize`) returns the previous run's committed state or the default, not the value just set.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a declaration from a task that outlives init can commit without its listener, and a read during the commit write shows the previous committed value.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a declaration from a task that outlives init can commit without its listener, and a read during the commit write shows the previous committed value.

findings.title: The Build note "`initial` column: nothing reads it back" is wrong
findings.why_it_matters: `parse_row` loads the column into `Declaration.initial`, and `restore_state` falls back to `default_state(row.declaration)` for a value that doesn't parse, which uses that stored `initial`. That restored default then fits at the next commit and is kept. So a switch with a corrupt stored value comes back as the previously declared `initial`, not the current declaration's. The data-integrity critic called the note accurate, but it missed this path. The note misleads anyone relying on it.
findings.recommended: A: Correct the Build note: the column is read back when a stored value doesn't parse, so such a switch restores to its previously declared `initial`.
findings.chosen: A: Correct the Build note: the column is read back when a stored value doesn't parse, so such a switch restores to its previously declared `initial`.

findings.title: A corrupt stored row for an instance that never commits again stays and warns on every boot
findings.why_it_matters: A row whose declaration doesn't parse is skipped at load with a WARNING; the instance's next commit rewrites it. A disabled or non-autostart app never commits, and it isn't pruned because it's still configured, so the same WARNING repeats at every start. If Finding 2's option A ships, an instance that declares nothing also never commits, since memory doesn't know about the skipped row.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: an unparseable row of an instance that never commits again warns at every start until the row is fixed or the instance is removed from config.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: an unparseable row of an instance that never commits again warns at every start until the row is fixed or the instance is removed from config.

findings.title: A failed rollback in the integration commit leaves the shared writer connection in an unknown state
findings.why_it_matters: `replace_instance_set` wraps its transaction in `except BaseException: safe_rollback`. `safe_rollback` logs and absorbs a storage error from the rollback itself, and its docstring says the connection's transaction state is then unknown, so the next `BEGIN` from any writer can fail. This is the existing retention pattern the ledger follows on purpose, but the integration commit makes it reachable at every app start (Finding 2).
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a commit whose rollback also fails leaves the writer connection's transaction state unknown, as for every other `safe_rollback` caller.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a commit whose rollback also fails leaves the writer connection's transaction state unknown, as for every other `safe_rollback` caller.
